11. The grounds taken in the application for the return of the plaint and the release of the vessel are that the plaint has not been signed either by the plaintiff or by a person duly authorised by the plaintiff. Secondly, the plaint does not disclose any cause of action to bring the suit within the scope of the Admiralty Act, 1861. Thirdly, that the plaintiff being an unpaid vendor had no scope to invoke the Admiralty Jurisdiction under section 6 of the Admiralty Act. 

 38. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq contended that there is no allegation that damage has been done to the goods carried into Bangladesh by the defendant vessel and further submits that in order to come within the scope of section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 there must be damage done to the goods. In support of his contention he cited the case of Eastern Steamship Enterprise Private Ltd. vs. Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute, reported in 35 DLR 414. The facts and circumstances of the case reported in 35 DLR 414 are however quite different. In the said suit plaintiff claimed as demurrage a sum of Taka 9,96,600.00 and a further sum of Taka 75,500.00 as incidental cost. And the Admiralty Court held "As the instant suit is not for damages done to the goods or any part thereof or for any breach of the contract on the part of the owner, master  crew of the ship the present case does not come within section 6." 

 Section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 reads as follows: 

 39. Accordingly, the word "Bangladesh is to be read for the words England and Wales in section 6 of the Act of 1861, in its application to this High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. 

 40. In a pure and simple suit for the realisation of the money by an unpaid vendor, admiralty jurisdiction cannot be invoked. To attract admiralty jurisdiction conditions as laid down in section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 are to be present. 

 44. In the case of National Co. Ltd. vs. Asia Mariner, reported in 72 CWN 635 while interpreting section 6 of the Admiralty Act 1861 it has been observed that the section has been liberally construed in the St. Cloud, 167 ER 269. The Norway 167 ER 347 and by the Privy Council in the Pieve Superior LR (1874) 5 PC 482 In the Peive Superior the Privy Council said "The statute being remedial of a grievance, by employing the jurisdiction of the Court of Admiralty Court, according to the general rule applicable to such statutes, to be construed liberally so as to afford the utmost relief which the fair meaning of its language will allow. 

 48. From the discussions made above I hold that the suit comes within the ambit of section 6 of the Admiralty Act, 1861.
